facts.claim: Benjamin Dakota Rogers released the album Better By Now on April 5, 2019. It has 11 tracks, and the title track opens it at 3:48.
Better by Now was digitally released as a single on January 25, 2019, ahead of the album. It earned a top 40 single spot on the Airplay Direct Folk chart.
All songs on the album were written by Benjamin Dakota Rogers. Dan Hosh produced it.

The album was recorded and mixed by Dan Hosh at Catherine North Studios in Hamilton, Ontario. Scott Peacock, Will Crann and Zach Gerber did additional engineering, and Ryan Morey mastered it in Montreal.

Discogs credits for the album list Dan Hosh on electric and Nashville guitar, mandolin, B3 organ and percussion. Kirk Starkey played cello, Peter Klaassen upright bass, and Chris Raitt, Jeff Heisholt and Mike Tudisco piano. Percussion came from Mike Tudisco, Samuel Keating and Scott Peacock.
Backing vocalists on the album include Chris Raitt, Chris Thompson, Dan Hosh, James DeGeer, Meg Contini, Nate Daniels and Will Crann.
The title track is described as a folk-pop ballad about the internal friction of making yourself swallow bitter truths and move on. Roots Music Report calls the album his fourth studio album.
The lead track was called a beautifully sad folk pop ballad by Folk Roots Radio's Jan Hall. It deals with realizing in a relationship that you 'really ought to know better by now'.
Rogers launched the album at Hugh's Room Live in Toronto on April 6, 2019. A press piece says it strips his sound down to its core.
Rogers inherited his great-grandfather's violin at age seven. He has described moving from fiddle player to singer-songwriter as an organic shift.

Rogers is a Canadian folk singer-songwriter. His albums run Wayfarer (2014), Strong Man's Address to the Circus Crowd (2015), Whisky & Pine (2016), Better by Now (2019), Paint Horse (2023) and This Ol' Way (2025). Paint Horse earned a Juno nomination for Traditional Roots Album of the Year.

research.lineage: Rogers is an Ontario singer-songwriter who grew up in the fiddle world on a farm, and this record sits in contemporary and alternative folk with roots, blues and country influences.

draft:
The stars in **Better by Now** are doing everyone else a favor. They're "Shining down like kerosene lights," guiding sailors home, sending sinners to bed, chasing the monsters out of somebody's head. Benjamin Dakota Rogers opens the song with that whole list of comforts, then turns around and admits none of it reaches him. "Ain't it funny" is how each verse begins, and it isn't funny. It's the wry shrug of someone who can see the cure working on everybody but himself.

That gap between knowing and doing is the whole song. The refrain says the same line three times, as if repetition might make it stick, and then gives up: "But damn it I don't." In the second chorus that surrender comes three times in a row before the "Yeah baby" closes it out. It sounds less like a lesson learned than a confession made in the open, the narrator embarrassed and still unwilling to pretend otherwise.

The second verse holds the sharpest moment. The narrator can't even say her name, because it hurts, and two lines later is talking straight to "you." The grief won't stay in the third person. Then comes the line that keeps him from simple blame, "you're not bad you're just bad for me," followed by an image of begging at her door like a hungry dog. Self-respect and longing sit right next to each other and neither one wins. The bridge drops the excuses and just reports what she promised: "You said I'd always be your home." Said twice, it lands as the real wound underneath the self-scolding.

The sound stays close and plain. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through an arpeggio over a steady bass note, and the tempo is slow enough to let each line breathe. Rogers sings in a mid-range voice with a little rasp, unadorned, with no harmonies to soften it. The recording is dry, like a small room, and in the stretch heard the arrangement doesn't build. It just holds steady, the way someone holds a thought they can't put down.

Rogers wrote it, and Dan Hosh produced the record at Catherine North Studios in Hamilton, Ontario. It opens the album of the same name. Rogers came up as a fiddle player before he became a singer-songwriter, and the song carries that roots-folk plainness, a ballad more interested in an honest sentence than an ornament.

It sticks because it says out loud the thing you'd rather keep to yourself: you know exactly what's bad for you, and you go back anyway.
